title: Top officer’s pay against the organization’s size and its City money
question: Where the City is a main funder, how does the top officer’s pay compare with organizations of like size, with the number of employees and with the City money received?
finding: The top officer’s pay could be set against size at 413 City-paid organizations; the middle figure runs from $95,746 for those with revenue under $1 million to $625,623 for those with $100 million or more. Of 186 for which the City supplied a quarter or more of revenue, 17 pay their top officer at least one and a half times the middle figure for their size. Furthest above: The Transgender Advocates For Justice An, $280,261 on revenue of $761,690 (2.9 times its peers; 37% of revenue), then San Francisco Clean City Coalition ($212,724, 2.2 times) and Arriba Juntos - Ial ($521,378, 1.9 times). At 21 of them, pay to all listed officers and key employees is a fifth or more of all spending, led by San Francisco Clean City Coalition (42%). At 1 more the listed pay is larger than everything the return says was spent, which points to pay carried by another body or to an error on the return rather than to high pay. 18 organizations whose top officer is paid mainly by a related organization are left out here and appear in the table on related organizations.
how: The latest return covering eleven months or more for each organization. The top officer is the best-paid current officer whose title says chief executive, executive director or president (failing that, the best-paid current officer); pay is the total on Part VII of the return, from the organization and related organizations. Organizations are grouped by revenue into six bands and each is set against the middle top-officer pay of its band, computed across all City-paid organizations with a return. Listed: those where City payments were at least 25% of revenue, ranked by pay against the band. “Pay to all listed people” adds up everyone on Part VII paid by the organization and divides by total expenses. City money is spread onto the tax year by days of overlap; for the two largest child-care voucher agencies it is taken from the child-care pages. Where the organization’s tax number was matched by hand and has not been verified, the last column says so.
limits: Pay is set by each board and no rule caps it; the tax rule is only that it be reasonable for the job. Revenue is a rough measure of the job: an organization that passes most of its money through to others, runs clinics with physicians, or manages buildings is harder or easier to lead than its revenue suggests. A small organization’s chief can be its main programme worker, so a high share of revenue is common there. Pay can include a one-time payout, and a year with two chief executives shows only one. The existing screen “Top pay where the City is the main funder” under people follows pay against revenue over time; this one compares across organizations.
